nodes.annotation: The oldest job in the schedule (jobid 7, versus 18-21 for the cron-auth-migrated set) and the only one that sends no auth header at all. It predates the RLS-hardening pass that set verify_jwt=true on refresh-symbols, and it was never migrated because no migration in the repo schedules it — it was created out-of-band, so the Phase 2b sweep over supabase/migrations/ never saw it. Its `symbols` target table is likewise created by no migration. IMPORTANT when diagnosing this: cron.job_run_details reports 'succeeded' for every run regardless, because net.http_post is asynchronous — the job status records that the request was ENQUEUED (return_message '1 row' is the request id), not what the server answered. Checked 2026-07-27: five consecutive 'succeeded' runs, which is exactly what a job 401ing every six hours also looks like. Use net._http_response, or check whether the symbols rows actually changed.

nodes.annotation: 1481 lines, and the only production caller is one cron job. Runs with verify_jwt=false, so the in-code constant-time apikey check is the entire authentication boundary — note it runs before the body parse and before the DB client is constructed, which is what makes an unauthenticated request cheap to reject. The two extracted modules are the parts that have been burned by bugs and are now pinned by hermetic unit tests.

nodes.annotation: The unmodernised twin of snapshot-week-start. Same cron-auth pattern, same Alpaca dependency, same table — but no extracted pure module and no test file. It is the highest-value cleanup target in the repo precisely because its failure mode is silent: bad week_end_price data does not throw, it just scores people wrong.

nodes.annotation: The batch key is (league_id, week_number), not league_id. Grouping by league alone meant a league with several unscored weeks scored every one of them against week[0]'s snapshots and trade window. The sort order is equally load-bearing: the handler advances current_week only when the batch's week equals the league's current week, so weeks must arrive ascending or a league gets permanently stuck.
nodes.label: grouping.ts

nodes.annotation: Pure decision functions — no side effects, no Deno APIs; every logging call and DB write stays in index.ts. The evaluation ORDER inside decideBatchScoring is part of the contract: freshness is checked before the week>1 rule, so a stale week>1 batch reports stale_no_snapshots (the actionable operational cause) rather than the generic reason. Swapping them would silently relabel every stale skip.

flows.title: Weekly scoring

steps.detail: net.http_post with an apikey header read from vault secret `cron_apikey`.
Job marked running before any work.
Pending matchups: team1_gain IS NULL, week_end in the past, league_type=matchup. The NULL filter is what makes a re-run idempotent.
One batch per (league_id, week_number), sorted week-ascending. Grouping by league alone was the original bug; the sort is load-bearing for week advancement.
Per batch. Presence of any row sets hasSnapshots; any week_end_price sets hasWeekEndPrices.

GUARDS 1 & 2 — decideBatchScoring. A snapshot-less batch is skipped whole: stale_no_snapshots (>72h) or no_snapshots_week_gt_1. Freshness is checked first, and that order is load-bearing for ops labelling.
Mid-week trades inside [weekStart, weekEnd], then a second read bounded to week_end so a post-week sale cannot empty holdings and flip a win to an auto-loss.
Fallback scorer input — only reachable at week 1.
Latest quotes, IEX feed. Failures are swallowed into an empty price map rather than throwing.
GUARD 3a — decideUserScorer picks full | legacy | fallback | unscoreable per user. A snapshot-less user past week 1 is unscoreable: cumulative-from-entry is all-time P/L, not a weekly delta.
GUARD 3b — decideMatchupScoring refuses any matchup containing an unscoreable participant. Byes gate on team1 only. Refused matchups keep team1_gain NULL and stay pending.
Winner written: bye = auto-win, empty portfolio = auto-loss, else dollar gain, tiebreak percent then playoff seed.
Read-then-increment, not transactional and NOT reversible. This irreversibility is the entire reason guards 1-3 refuse rather than fabricate.
current_week re-read per batch and advanced only when the batch IS the current week — so a guard-skipped week blocks advancement instead of being stepped over.
Season end, from playoffs finals or from standings when playoff_teams = 0.

flows.annotation: The most defensive path in the codebase, and the reason it is defensive is that league_standings increments are irreversible. There is no transaction around the read-then-increment and no compensating write, so a fabricated score cannot be undone by re-running. Three guards therefore refuse rather than guess. Read them in order: decideBatchScoring kills a whole snapshot-less league-week; decideUserScorer marks an individual snapshot-less user unscoreable past week 1; decideMatchupScoring refuses any matchup containing one. All three exist because the fallback scorer returns cumulative-from-draft-entry P/L, which is only a valid weekly delta in week 1.

steps.detail: net.http_post with apikey from vault `cron_apikey`.

Historical bars for week-start prices.
ALL-OR-NOTHING per league-week with completeness-based skip (fixed in 2caf9f8). A partial price fetch writes nothing rather than a half-week.
Retry scheduling, shared with snapshot-week-end.

flows.annotation: Read this against flow.week-start-snapshot — the asymmetry is the point. snapshot-week-start has an extracted, unit-tested plan.ts and was hardened in 2caf9f8 to write all-or-nothing per league-week with a completeness-based skip. snapshot-week-end has neither: no extracted module, no tests, and its write path has not been audited for the same partial-write defect. Both feed the same week_snapshots rows that weekly scoring reads, and week-end runs only ten minutes before scoring does.

flows.title: Place a trade

trigger.detail: User confirms a buy or sell in TradeModal

steps.detail: Live quote for the symbol before confirming.
Order submitted server-side so broker credentials never reach the client.
Per-user Alpaca keys read server-side.
Order placed against the user's own Alpaca account. place-order does NOT touch the trades table — it returns the Alpaca order to the client.

The trade row is written by the CLIENT after place-order returns — not server-side. So the DB record and the real Alpaca order are committed by two different actors with no transaction between them: if the app dies in this gap the order exists at the broker and not in the DB. That gap is why order reconciliation exists.

flows.annotation: The trade row is written by the client, not by place-order. place-order reads broker_credentials, submits to Alpaca, and returns; TradeModal then inserts into trades. The broker order and the database record are committed by two different actors with nothing linking them transactionally, so a crash, network drop, or backgrounded app between the two leaves a real position at Alpaca with no row in the DB. flow.order-reconciliation exists to close that window after the fact.

flows.title: Season reset

trigger.detail: Commissioner taps reset in league settings

steps.detail: Called directly from the client as an authenticated user. EXECUTE is granted to `authenticated`, so the authorization is NOT the grant — it is an INTERNAL commissioner check inside the function body. That gate is the only thing standing between any league member and a destructive season reset.

flows.annotation: The only flow where a destructive operation is authorized entirely inside a function body. EXECUTE on start_new_league_season is granted to `authenticated`, so any logged-in user can call it with any league id. Nothing in the grant layer stops a non-commissioner from resetting someone else's league — the internal commissioner check is the whole control. That is deliberate (the client calls it directly, so it must be authenticated-callable), but it means the gate has to be correct, with no defence in depth if it regresses.
